::: post-intro
Last March Seabra's had whole brisket on sale, so I bought one. I decided to smoke one up for Father's day, with delicious consquences.
:::

The first thing I learned was that “whole” in the circular means **WHOLE**, as in, the whole cut and not sliced into family-sized portions. But they were nice enough to cut it into pieces, which went straight into my freezer.

[Brisket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brisket) is the cut of beef from which corned beef is made. This is what I kept telling my kids, because they love corned beef but they wrinkled their noses at the sound of the word “brisket.” Smoked brisket as barbecue is popular in Texas, where they have always had plenty of excess beef.

After defrosting I rubbed the piece down with the southern dry rub for [barbecue from the Joy of Cooking](http://www.thejoykitchen.com/recipe/faux-smoked-pulled-pork). Active ingredients: paprika, cumin, salt, pepper, brown sugar. It happened to be in the refrigerator.

<figure class="img-responsive, img-thumbnail">
<img src="https://c7.staticflickr.com/8/7079/27188187174_8aeef7482b_z.jpg" class="img-responsive, img-thumbnail" alt="Brisket, dry rubbed" />
<figcaption aria-hidden="true">Brisket, dry rubbed</figcaption>
</figure>

I put in on the grill about 6:00am. On one side, the heat. I used an iron smoker box full of hickory wood chips that had soaked overnight. On the other side, the meat. I put an aluminum pan under the brisket, and poured in the water than the chips had soaked in.

I kept it on there for just over 10 hours at about 250 degrees. I didn't get a whole lot of smoke from the chips. I've had better results with a foil packet.

When I took it out it was nice and barky. The thermometer read 165 on the bottom and 175-180 near the top. I know that 190 is the magic number to break down meat, but I wanted to give it time to rest, and I was really afraid of it being dry. Plus I've never owned a thermometer that I had complete faith in.

<figure class="img-responsive, img-thumbnail">
<img src="https://c6.staticflickr.com/8/7041/27724902101_bf2770d65d_z.jpg" class="img-responsive, img-thumbnail" alt="Brisket, smoked" />
<figcaption aria-hidden="true">Brisket, smoked</figcaption>
</figure>

After this I tried the “[FTC](http://bbqdictionary.com/foil-towel-cooler/)” method they rave about on the BBQ forums. FTC stands for *foil*, *towel*, *cooler.* It is a method for resting meat that keeps it from cooling down too much. Resting meat is important to let the juices distribute evenly, but let it rest on the counter for too long and it will get too cool to enjoy.

You usually think of a cooler as something to keep things cold. But it's just an insulator, and not smart enough to know the difference between keeping heat from coming in versus keeping heat from getting out. So something warm in the cooler stays warm (not forever—the contents will tend towards room temperature, just like they would if they were cold.) The foil keeps the juices from escaping, and the towel provides further insulation.

I wrapped the meat up tightly and bundled it in two old dishtowels (you don't want to risk leaking greasy beef juice on good towels). I managed to get it in one of Igloo Playmate coolers that holds about a sixpack. I figured the snug fit would be better for heat retention.

For sides, I made some Texas-style pinto beans and cornbread. Neither were sweetened, as you might find with southern barbecue. Also a cucumber salad with dill and a red wine vinaigrette.

When I took the brisket out of the cooler and sliced it, I know it was going to be heavenly. The knife went right through the top half (the “point”) with very little resistance. The bottom (“flat”) was a little less tender, but I kept the slices think and across the grain. They glistened with juice and fat rendered from the center ribbon.

Served!

Still life, with High Life.

I had forgotten to put any sauce on before I took this photo. To be honest, it almost wasn't necessary, the slices were so juicy. But I had made one, by reducing some of the separated pan juices with bottled barbecue sauce (Dinosaur Barbecue's Sensuous Slathering, if you must know.) And it was good.

Maybe next time I'll use multiple foil packets so I can keep the smoke going. But this one is definitely a keeper.
